Learning Objectives

Plan perioperative care for patients with inflammatory arthritis.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy of Rheumatoid Arthritis
Overview
Inflammatory arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disease.
Rheumatoid arthritis is characterized by synovitis, ligamentous laxity, cartilage destruction,
and periarticular bone loss of multiple joints.




Overview
Rheumatoid arthritis is a type of inflammatory arthritis. Although most ankle arthritis is
posttraumatic, rheumatoid arthritis is related to autoimmune disease, in which the
inflammatory process directly attacks the joints. This process includes synovitis, the
development of ligamentous laxity, cartilage destruction, and periarticular bone loss of
many joints.
Epidemiology
The prevalence of rheumatoid arthritis is higher in women and in individuals from the United
States and northern European countries.

Epidemiology
Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with a prevalence of 0.5% to 1% in the United States
and northern Europe.1 Rheumatoid arthritis affects women at approximately twice the
rate of men.2 Almost all patients with rheumatoid arthritis will eventually have foot or
ankle problems. Between 20% and 50% of patients have foot or ankle symptoms as the
presenting symptom for rheumatoid arthritis.3,4
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Rheumatoid arthritis preferentially attacks the small joints of the feet and hands.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The classically described findings of rheumatoid arthritis involve the small joints of the
feet and hands. In the hands, this results in ulnar deviation. Rheumatoid arthritis
particularly attacks the metacarpophalangeal joints in the hands and the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:18 AM
AAOS | Inflammatory Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000003
2/21

metatarsophalangeal joints in the feet. Rheumatoid arthritis may lead to subluxation as
the synovitis attacks the joints. This is particularly observed in the forefoot, leading to
forefoot deformities with hallux valgus, which shifts weight bearing laterally to the lesser
metatarsals, creating metatarsalgia.5 (Resource 1).

Etiology
The actual cause of rheumatoid arthritis is unknown. Genetic and environmental factors
are suspected.4 Rheumatoid is four times more likely to occur in patients with an
identical twin who has rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is associated the
human lymphocyte antigen DR4, and a viral infection has been hypothesized to initiate
the disease.4
Natural History
The incidence of foot problems increases the longer a patient has rheumatoid arthritis.6

Natural History
Rheumatoid arthritis can follow one of three courses. It may be progressive and
destructive without remission, monocyclic with a single incident of synovitis, or
polycyclic. The polycyclic course is the most common (70%), in which patients experience
repetitive flares of the synovium followed by periods of remission.4 In patients with
chronic rheumatoid arthritis, symmetric involvement typically is observed. Early in the
disease process the patient may have asymmetric involvement.
Risk Factors
Family history

Classification
Classification based on physical examination and radiographs (Table 1)

ed 9. Philadelphia, PA, Saunders, 2014, pp 867-1007.

Classification
Rheumatoid arthritis of the foot and ankle is categorized into four stages. These stages
are based on physical examination findings and radiographs. Stage I is defined
discomfort and synovitis without radiographic changes. In stage II, early radiographic
erosive changes are observed and a deformity begins to develop; however, the
deformity remains flexible. In stage III, patients develop fixed soft-tissue deformities and
radiographs demonstrate extensive erosive changes of the joints. In the fourth and final
stage, severe, fixed deformities, including hallux valgus; lesser metatarsophalangeal joint
dislocations; lesser toe deformities with hammering or clawing; pes planovalgus; and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:18 AM
AAOS | Inflammatory Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000003
4/21

midfoot arthritis are present and radiographs demonstrate these deformities and
articular destruction.
Evaluation/Diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis
Patient History
Patients often report diffuse joint pain, particularly of the forefoot.

Patient History
Early in the disease process, patients will have the most pain in the forefoot, and it may
include a subtle synovitis without radiographic changes (stage I). Later in the disease
process, patients will have pain related to fixed deformities and may report inability to
find accommodative footwear.
Physical Examination
Synovitis and inflammation are early diagnostic findings.

Physical Examination
Early in the arthritic process, physical examination may reveal minimal findings and
require a high level of suspicion. Later in the disease process, deformities related to the
synovitis occur. Forefoot deformities are classic, including hallux valgus, subluxation or
dislocation of the lesser metatarsophalangeal joints, and hammer toe or claw toe
deformities of the lesser toes. Often, patients also exhibit valgus deviation of the lesser
metatarsals.
Imaging Studies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:18 AM
AAOS | Inflammatory Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000003
5/21

Radiography
Radiographs will demonstrate periarticular erosions and symmetric joint space narrowing,
with later radiographs demonstrating the development of deformities.

Radiography
Early in the disease process, radiographs may not demonstrate any changes. As
rheumatoid arthritis progresses, radiographs will demonstrate periarticular erosions and
symmetric joint space narrowing. As moderate disease progresses, the characteristic
forefoot deformities develop: hallux valgus, subluxation or dislocation of the lesser
metatarsophalangeal joints, and hammer toe or claw toe deformities of the lesser toes.
Just as the hands demonstrate ulnar deviation, the lesser toes often demonstrate valgus
deviation. Isolated talonavicular joint arthritis is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and
other inflammatory arthropathies.
Laboratory Findings
Characteristic laboratory findings include rheumatoid factor, antibodies to anti- cyclic
citrullinated peptides, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
level.8

Laboratory Findings
Most patients with rheumatoid arthritis have positive laboratory tests for rheumatoid
factor and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptides. In addition, most patients with
rheumatoid arthritis also have an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-
reactive protein level. However, 30% to 40% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis have
negative laboratory tests for rheumatoid factor or antibodies to cyclic citrullinated
peptides or a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein level.

Therefore, laboratory studies are yet the preferred method for diagnosis or monitoring
treatment.

Diagnosis
In 2010, the American College of Rheumatology and the European League Against
Rheumatism created classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis. This classification
system was developed to classify rheumatoid arthritis in newly presenting patients. The
criteria include factors such as number of large and small joints involved, serology
studies, acute-phase reactants, and the duration of symptoms9 (Table 2).

ACPA = anti-citrullinated protein antibody, CRP = C-reactive protein, ESR = erythrocyte
sedimentation rate, RF = rheumatoid factor, RH = rheumatoid arthritis.
a The criteria are aimed at classification of newly presenting patients. In addition,
patients with erosive disease typical of RA with a history compatible with prior fulfillment
of the 2010 criteria should be classified as having RA. Patients with longstanding disease,
including those with disease that is inactive (with or without treatment) who, based on
retrospectively available data, have previously fulfilled the 2010 criteria should be
classified as having RA.
b Differential diagnoses vary among patients with different presentations, but may
include conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, psoriatic arthritis, and gout. If
relevant differential diagnoses to consider are unclear, then an expert rheumatologist
should be consulted.
c Although patients with a score of =6/10 are not classifiable as having RA, their status
can be reassessed and the criteria may be fulfilled cumulatively over time.
dJoint involvement refers to any swollen or tender joint on examination, which may be
confirmed via imaging evidence of synovitis. Distal interphalangeal joints, first
carpometacarpal joints, and first metatarsophalangeal joints are excluded from
assessment. Categories of joint distribution are classified according to the location and
number of involved joints, with placement into the highest category possible based on
the pattern of joint involvement.

f Small joints refers to the metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints,
second through fifth metatarsophalangeal joints, thumb interphalangeal joints, and
wrists.
g At least one of the involved joints must be a small joint; the other joints can include any

h Negative refers to International unit (IU) values that are less than or equal to the upper
limit of normal (ULN) for the laboratory and assay; low-positive refers to IU values that
are higher than the ULN but =3 times the ULN for the laboratory and assay; high-positive
refers to IU values that are =3 times the ULN for the laboratory and assay. If RF
information is only available as positive or negative, a positive result should be scored as
low-positive for RF.
i Normal/abnormal is determined by local laboratory standards.

The differential diagnosis for rheumatoid arthritis is broad. It includes other
autoimmune disorders, viral polyarthropathies, osteoarthritis, and seronegative
arthropathies.
Management of Rheumatoid Arthritis
Nonsurgical Management
Management follows treatment algorithms for specific joints.
Involvement of a rheumatologist is paramount to help modify the course of the disease.

Nonsurgical Management
The surgical management of rheumatoid arthritis depends on which joints are involved
and the degree of arthritis and deformity. The involvement of a medical specialist who
manages arthritis with disease-modifying medications is required.
Surgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Treatment options are joint specific

Techniques/Procedures
Surgical treatment options for the management of rheumatoid arthritis are joint specific.
Two surgical treatment options merit additional discussion. First, because of the unique
role of synovial destruction in driving rheumatoid arthritis, synovectomy is a reasonable
treatment option in patients without substantial joint disease or malalignment.10
Second, in patients with hallux valgus, metatarsophalangeal joint arthrodesis is
preferred for the management of first metatarsophalangeal joint deformity because of
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000003
10/21

the progressive nature of the disease. The classic correction is metatarsophalangeal
arthrodesis and resection arthroplasty of the lesser toe deformities.
Preoperative Planning
Perioperative coordination with the patient’s rheumatologist is mandatory.

Preoperative Planning
Some disease-modifying medications may be continued in the perioperative period (eg,
methotrexate), whereas other medications must be be stopped for any moderate or
intensive procedure (eg, tumor necrosis factor antagonists)11 (Resource 2).
A general guide to continuing or stopping disease-modifying medications is provided in
Table 3. Metabolic bone health should be evaluated, given that many patients have been
treated with the use of steroids and have decreased mobility because of joint pain. The
disease itself also may result in osteoporosis.12

Complications
Complications that can occur after surgical management are generally specific to the
treatment modality chosen. Rheumatoid therapeutic agents do not seem to be
associated with healing or postoperative complications of the foot and ankle.13,14
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy of Psoriatic Arthritis and Other
Seronegative Arthropathies
Overview
Seronegative spondyloarthropathies are a group of overlapping disorders.

Overview
Psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis are the most common seronegative
spondyloarthropathies. These conditions share features, such as frequent involvement
of other organ systems, absence of rheumatoid factor, and increased frequency of
human leukocyte antigen B27 variants.15
Epidemiology
The prevalence of psoriatic arthritis ranges from 0.02% to 0.25%.


Epidemiology
Psoriasis is more prevalent than psoriatic arthritis. The estimated prevalence of psoriasis
ranges from 0.6% to 4.8%, whereas the estimated prevalence of psoriatic arthritis ranges
from 0.02% to 0.25%. An even distribution exists between men and women, and the
typical onset occurs in patients in their thirties.16
Etiology
Psoriatic arthritis is associated with a genetic component.

Etiology
The genetics of psoriatic arthritis are not yet completely understood; however, a clear
genetic component has been noted. Human leukocyte antigen B27 variants are
associated with all seronegative arthropathies. In addition, population-based studies
show that obesity increases the risk of psoriatic arthritis in patients with psoriasis.17,18
Risk Factors
Family history of psoriasis

Classification
The Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis can be used to aid in the diagnosis of
psoriatic arthritis. Points are assigned based on evidence of psoriasis, family history,
presence of nail lesions, negative rheumatoid factor, dactylitis, and periostitis16 (Table
4).

Evaluation/Diagnosis of Psoriatic Arthritis and Other
Seronegative Arthropathies
History
Personal or family history of psoriasis

History
Psoriatic arthritis should be suspected in all patients with a history of psoriasis who have
new onset joint pain. Patients often report diffuse pain, which may or may not be
symmetric. A family history also is concerning for seronegative arthropathy.
Physical Examination
Nail changes and dactylitis are classic physical examination findings.


Physical Examination
The physical examination is crucial in evaluating for psoriatic arthritis and other
seronegative arthropathies. Symmetric joint swelling and phenomena such as morning
stiffness should increase suspicion of an autoimmune disease. For psoriatic arthritis,
psoriatic lesions or nail lesions (including pits or oncholysis) also are concerning for
disease. Finally, dactylitis (sausage digits) often is observed.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Psoriatic arthritis leads to a classic pencil-in-cup deformity on radiographs.

Radiography
In psoriatic arthritis, the joint appears to be a pencil within a cup because of periarticular
erosions and bone resorption. This deformity also may be observed in patients with
rheumatoid arthritis, reactive arthritis, or systemic sclerosis; however, is classically
associated with psoriatic arthritis (Figure 1).

Rheumatoid arthritis


Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for psoriatic arthritis and seronegative arthritis is broad. It
includes other autoimmune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis, as well as viral
polyarthropathies, other rheumatoid diseases, and osteoarthritis.
Management of Psoriatic Arthritis and Other Seronegative
Arthropathies

Nonsurgical Management
The management of psoriatic arthritis and seronegative arthropathies always should
begin with nonsurgical management via disease-modifying medications. Supportive
management via bracing is a helpful adjunct for the foot and the ankle. Involvement of a
rheumatologist is paramount to help modify the course of the disease.

Surgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Specific surgical techniques depend on joint involvement.
Preoperative Planning
Perioperative coordination with the patient’s rheumatologist is mandatory.
Skin involvement must be considered.

Preoperative Planning
Some disease-modifying medications may be continued in the perioperative period (eg,
methotrexate), whereas other medications should be stopped for any moderate or
intensive procedure (eg, tumor necrosis factor antagonists).11 Dermatologists should be
consulted preoperatively if the patient has active skin disease, because psoriatic plaques
harbor increased amounts of bacteria. If possible, the surgeon should avoid incising
through a psoriatic plaque. Finally, preoperative evaluation should include testing for
diabetes mellitus because a relationship exists between psoriasis and obesity.
Complications
Complications are specific to the treatment modality selected.
